cells.tense: The pull is here now because something you built has finished, not because you reached for it
cells.act: trace the pattern across the last few times
cells.ask: Walk back through a few recent times you moved toward something you wanted — where each pull came from, what it turned out to want — and read the shape off them yourself.
cells.core:
The draw is clean right now. Something you stayed with has finished, and the light coming off it is real rather than conjured. In yourself you can tell this apart from a version you'd have to talk yourself into. That difference is the whole tell.

It holds as long as you keep looking under the surface. Walk back through a few recent times you moved toward something you wanted — where each pull came from, what it turned out to want — and read the shape off them yourself. That is what keeps the aim honest instead of decorative. Whatever you build next has this as its floor.
cells.sheetLine: You shine from what you finished, not what you reached for.
cells.verb: steering by what you actually want, not by what you can imagine wanting
cells.place: the moment you look at what's ahead and decide whether to move toward it

cells.tense: You are already arranging the brightness of a morning that hasn't arrived yet
cells.act: wait until you know which part matters, then begin with that part
cells.ask: Before you commit to the next bright plan, hold off until the part that actually matters is clear — then start with only that, and leave the rest for later.
cells.core:
The pull is outrunning everything that could catch up to it — brightness arranged for a morning that hasn't arrived. From the outside it reads as shine; from in close it's bracing. The dazzle is there because you want the arrival to be certain, and certainty feels like a hedge against the wait.

Nothing needs retracting. Before you commit to the next bright plan, hold off until the part that actually matters is clear — then start with only that, and leave the rest for later. That's not second-guessing. It's letting what you already sense decide the order. The light doesn't need switching on early for it to be real later.
cells.sheetLine: You're lighting tomorrow before tomorrow has a shape.

cells.tense: You kept at the work and the flowering didn't come, so the aim went quiet with it
cells.act: give it what it needs today, not what it is scheduled for
cells.ask: Take something you still care about — a plant, a page, a person — and this week give it the water, the hour, or the rest it needs today rather than what you'd planned.
cells.core:
The pull toward what you want has gone quiet. You kept at it and the flowering didn't come, the door you were walking toward is behind you now, and caring for what's growing has stopped being something you do. The aim you used to move by reads as a thing that once embarrassed you.

Start again at the smallest scale. Take something you still care about — a plant, a page, a person — and this week give it the water, the hour, or the rest it needs today rather than what you'd planned. Doing that much is the whole instruction. If nothing comes of it, you still did the feeding, and the pull returns through the feeding before it returns any other way.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped tending. Start with something too small to fail.
cells.verb: steering by what you actually want, not by what you can imagine wanting

cells.tense: You are already giving off light, and you've been signing it to someone else
cells.act: keep it at its real size when you are asked to shrink it
cells.ask: Next time someone frames what you're doing as smaller than it is, say the true scope once, without arguing the point, and stay at that size.
cells.core:
There's light coming off work you've finished, and you've been handing the credit to luck, to timing, to someone else's pull. Ask and you'd say the draw is still ahead of you — that the real thing hasn't started yet. It has. You just haven't been signing for it.

Put your hand on the record. Next time someone frames what you're doing as smaller than it is, say the true scope once, without arguing the point, and stay at that size. You're not inflating anything. You're letting the acknowledgment catch up to something that was already true, and keeping your name on it while it does.
cells.sheetLine: The light is already yours. Sign for it.

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim is the specific content underneath the Too Little exhaustion — the record says hope was defeated by experience but not what happened, how long, or who; the draft stays on the condition (a door already behind them) without narrating the loss. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not exhausted, just quiet' or 'that doesn't describe my life', so every cell must land as a recognition offered, never a verdict, and the ask must be useful even if the read is wrong — each ask is one small doable act, not a fix. The sentence that served me more than them would be the diagnosis-sounding line 'you're running on empty', which I've cut; what remains is what the person can push back on and still use. The four asks open on four different verbs: trade, wait, tend, keep.
